title: Pauri 4, sound: saachaa saahib
hookLine: saachaa saahib saach naae bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar

cards: Back in camp three came an alarm set five minutes early for the amrit vela, the nectar hour before dawn. That hour came from somewhere specific: this pauri, the fourth step of Japji.

Before the early hours, though, hear how it begins. Its first line has a sound you already know: sach, the true, from aad sach, turns up twice, in two different forms, like one word trying on two coats.

teach.b: The opening line: saachaa saahib, saach naae, bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar. Saachaa: SAA-chaa, the true one. Saahib: SAA-hib, Master, Lord; the same sahib you hear in Japji Sahib and Guru Granth Sahib, a word of honor.
Saach: the true again, this time about a name. Naae: NAA-ay, name. Bhaakhiaa: BHAA-khi-aa, spoken, expressed.
Bhaau: rhymes with how, with a breath on the b; it means love. Apaar: a-PAAR, without limit, boundless. So the outline is already there: true Master, true name, spoken with boundless love.

Now the sound. Saachaa, saahib, saach: the line opens with three s-sounds in a row, soft and steady, like someone walking up to a door. Then bhaakhiaa bhaau, two bh sounds side by side, and the wide, open vowel of apaar.
From a narrow door into a very big room. Soon the pauri turns to questions: what can we offer, what words can we say?
Then a line you've heard before: amrit vela sach naau vadiaaee veechaar, the early hours, the true name, reflecting on its greatness.
Then a word that opens tomorrow: nadar. For now, this first line is almost a whole prayer in miniature: who the One is, what the Name is, and how it's spoken, with love and no limit.

how: The fourth pauri of Japji is recited each morning; its line on the amrit vela is the scriptural root of the Sikh practice of rising before dawn for simran.

o: out of reach, far away from us
on the far shore, across the river

games.q: match the sound to its sense.

s: the amrit vela comes from Japji's fourth pauri
amrit vela sach naau vadiaaee veechaar.
saahib in this line is unrelated to Japji Sahib
it's the same word of honor: Master, Lord.
the first line uses the word for true only once
saachaa, saach: the true appears in more than one form.

games.q: the first line says the true Master's name is spoken a certain way. how?
games.why: bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar: spoken with love that has no limit.

practice: Speak the first line softly: saachaa saahib, saach naae, bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar. Twice more, slower, the s-sounds soft and the last word open wide, then almost whispered.
Then sit, notice how your breath lengthened on apaar, and let it stay long; if you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Apaar. Boundless, without limit: how this pauri says love is spoken, saachaa saahib, true Master, true name.

orig.s: ਸਾਚਾ ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਸਾਚੁ ਨਾਇ ਭਾਖਿਆ ਭਾਉ ਅਪਾਰੁ
orig.say: SAA-chaa SAA-hib, SAACH NAA-ay, BHAA-khi-aa BHAU a-PAAR
orig.note: Gurmukhi: the opening line of Japji's fourth pauri, Ang 2.

carryVoice: Your line: saachaa saahib. The nectar hour before dawn starts in this pauri. Day one hundred sixty-nine, done.
